source_text: O lucens aurum in stercore! Quid verius, quid plenius dici a quoquam vel orthodoxo potuisset? Peccatum est, inquis, voluntas admittendi vel retinendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere [n41] . Ostendit hoc Ecclesiasticus: Deus, inquit, fecit hominem, et dimisit eum in manibus consilii sui; posuit ante eum vitam et mortem, aquam et ignem; quod placuerit ei, dabitur illi [n42] . Et per Isaiam Deus: Si volueritis, inquit, et audieritis me, quae bona sunt terrae edetis. Si nolueritis, nec audieritis, gladius vos comedet [n43] . Et Apo olus: Resipiscite iuste, et nolite peccare [n44] ; atque iterum: Nolite errare; Deus non irridetur; quae enim seminaverit homo, illa et metet [n45] .
pass_a_gloss: O gold shining in dung! What truer, what fuller thing could have been said by anyone even orthodox? Sin is, you say, a will of admitting or retaining what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. Ecclesiasticus shows this: God, he says, made the human, and sent him away in the hands of his own counsel; he placed before him life and death, water and fire; what will have pleased him will be given to him. And through Isaiah God: If you shall have willed, he says, and shall have heard me, you will eat the good things of the land. If you shall have been unwilling, and shall not have heard, the sword will eat you. And the Apostle: Come back to your senses justly, and do not will to sin; and again: Do not will to err; God is not mocked; for what a human shall have sown, those things he will also reap.

pass_b_english: What shining gold in a heap of dung! What could anyone, even an orthodox believer, have said more truly or more completely? “Sin”, you say, “is the will to commit or retain something justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain” (Augustine, On Two Souls 15). Ecclesiasticus shows this: “God made the human being and left him in the hands of his own decision. He placed before him life and death, water and fire; whatever pleases him will be given to him” (Sirach 15:14, 16–17; Vulgate 15:14, 17–18). And God says through Isaiah: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land. If you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword will devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). And the apostle: “Come rightly to your senses, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34). And again: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7–8).

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
